explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says what you sow "…is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else." (1 Corinthians 15:37). Nobody plants a seed and expects to see that same little seed standing there in July. The seed is just where it starts.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He says what you sow "…is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else." (1 Corinthians 15:37). The seed is not the finished body. Picture a lump of dough that hasn't met the oven yet: nobody calls that a cookie, and I'd know.

That's it, baker. Paul says "…God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body." (1 Corinthians 15:38). The farmer drops the seed and walks off. The body is God's doing.

A farmer does the sowing, friend, but look at who Paul credits. He says "…God gives it a body as He has designed…" (1 Corinthians 15:38). The farmer drops the seed in the dirt and waits like the rest of us. Paul gives the giving of the body to God.

Rain is a nice guess, friend, and no seed is complaining about a good drink. But Paul names someone else: "…God gives it a body as He has designed…" (1 Corinthians 15:38). He gives each kind of seed its own body. The rain doesn't get the credit.

Right, baker. Paul says, "Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). That's one list with four kinds in it. Each group keeps its own kind of flesh, so nobody in that lineup gets mixed up with the others.

Paul sees it differently, friend. He says, "Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). That's four kinds, not one. A bird and a fish are not wearing the same thing.

explanations.answer: Men and animals share one kind
explanations.explanation: Close, but Paul keeps them apart, friend. He says, "Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). Men get one kind and animals get another. Every group in his list has its own.

Look up again, friend. Paul says "The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor." (1 Corinthians 15:41). Sun, moon and stars each get their own. Even one star differs from the next.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor." (1 Corinthians 15:41). So the sun, the moon and the stars each have their own, and one star even differs from the next. My own night sky is full of stars, so I've had plenty of time to look.

You got it, baker. Paul says, "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). Perishable means it can wear out. Imperishable means it won't. Picture a cookie that never goes stale, and you're close to the idea.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). The body is not raised the same as it was sown. Something new has happened to it.

Nothing in the verse says anything about being unseen, friend. Paul says, "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). Imperishable is the word he picks. It's about a body that doesn't wear out.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). Dishonor on one side, glory on the other. Quite a swing, and he's not done, because the same verse goes on to say sown in weakness, raised in power.

I see why you'd go there, friend, since it sits near dishonor. But Paul says, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). He's not stacking one low word on another. He's flipping it around.
Paul has a louder word than that, friend. He says, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). Glory is the opposite of dishonor. Silence never makes it into the verse.

That's the one, baker. Paul says, "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). Then he adds, "If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). He treats the second as just as real as the first.

Paul draws a line between the two, friend. He says, "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). Sown is natural. Raised is spiritual. Using the same word twice wouldn't make much of a contrast.

Dust comes up later in the passage, friend, but not here. Paul says, "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). The raised body is a spiritual one. Hold onto that dust thought for a minute.
Yes, baker. Paul says, "the last Adam a life-giving spirit." (1 Corinthians 15:45). The first man Adam became a living being. The last Adam gives life.

That one belongs to the first Adam, friend. Paul says the first man Adam became a living being, and the last Adam is "…a life-giving spirit." (1 Corinthians 15:45). The two Adams get two different descriptions. For the last Adam, Paul's word is that He gives life.

Earth does come up, friend, but it's a different Adam. Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). For the last Adam, verse 45 says "…a life-giving spirit." I'd mix those up too if I were rushing through the batch.

Right, baker. Paul says, "The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual." (1 Corinthians 15:46). That's the order. Natural comes first, and the spiritual comes after, a bit like mixing the dough before the oven gets its turn.
Paul says it the other way around, friend. He says "The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual." (1 Corinthians 15:46). Natural comes first. The spiritual follows.
That's right, baker. Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). Dust for one, heaven for the other. Two very different starting points.

Eden is a fair guess, friend, since Adam is in the neighborhood. But Paul says, "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). He names heaven for the second man. Eden isn't in this verse.

Egypt is a long way off from this passage, friend. Paul says "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). The second man is from heaven. No road trip needed.

Careful, friend. Paul says, "…flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:50). He doesn't say it can, just as it is. Right after that, he says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51).

Yes, baker. Paul says, "…flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:50). The perishable can't inherit the imperishable. That's why the very next verse matters, where Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51).
That's it, baker. Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). Some sleep and some don't, but nobody is left out of the change. All of us means all of us.

Not in this verse, friend. Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). The word he uses is changed. He opens it with "Listen, I tell you a mystery…" and then names the change.

This mystery isn't a warning, friend. Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). The word is changed. He opens with "Listen, I tell you a mystery…" and then tells them what's coming.

explanations.answer: In the twinkling of an eye
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says it happens "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). That's the whole change, and he gives it no more time than an instant. I can't even find my oven mitts that quick.

explanations.answer: At the turning of a year
explanations.explanation: Way too slow, friend. Paul says "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). A year would be a very long wait. Paul says instant.

explanations.answer: In the passing of a day
explanations.explanation: Still too slow, friend. Paul says "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). A day is a whole lot of waiting. Paul says an instant, and he means it.

That's right, baker. Paul says "…the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Paul talks about being clothed, like putting on something new. Mortal gets covered by immortality.

Honor is a good guess, friend, since Paul said dishonor back in verse 43. Here he says, "For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Mortal pairs with immortality. Honor belongs to another verse.

Strength is a good guess, friend, since Paul spoke of weakness and power earlier (1 Corinthians 15:43). But in this verse he says, "For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Mortal is paired with immortality.

explanations.answer: It is swallowed up in victory
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says a saying that is written will come to pass: "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Death is the one getting swallowed. Not the other way around, and I'd say that's a good thing to know.

explanations.answer: It is held back for a season
explanations.explanation: Paul gives a different ending, friend. The saying is "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Nothing in it mentions a season. It says death is swallowed up, and Paul says that saying will come to pass.

explanations.answer: It is cast out of the land
explanations.explanation: No land in this one, friend. Paul says a saying that is written will come to pass: "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Swallowed up is the picture the saying gives. Nobody gets sent anywhere in it.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). He names sin as the sting of death. Then he adds that the power of sin is the law, all in one verse.
Fear is a good guess, friend, since death can sure feel scary. But Paul says "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). The text names sin, not fear.
Pain makes sense to guess, friend, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). Sin is the sting, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: Their labor in the Lord is not in vain
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Paul says, "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain means it counts. So keep those ovens warm.

explanations.answer: Others will see their good work
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason, friend. He says, "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). The reason he names is that the labor is not in vain.

explanations.answer: Their reward will come in this life
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say when anything comes, friend, and he doesn't give that reason. He says, "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain is the reason he gives.
